speaker: YOU
text: [whispering, tense] It's two a.m. [pause] Why is my heart going this fast?

speaker: YOU
text: [rushed, spiralling] I have the meeting, and the rent, and I didn't answer her text, and what if she's— and—

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [softly, cutting in gently] Hey. Hey. You know this feeling.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Everyone does. [slower] Tight chest. Racing thoughts. That low hum under everything that never quite switches off.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [matter-of-fact] We even have a word for it.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [conspiratorial, a hint of a smile] Here's the strange part. A hundred years ago, if you'd told a doctor you were "stressed", they wouldn't have pictured you. They'd have pictured a BRIDGE.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [warming up, quicker] Stress was an engineering word — the load on a steel beam, the strain on a cable. Then one clumsy young scientist borrowed it, and gave it to all of us.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [lower] And somebody paid him to keep saying it.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [beat, then warm and direct] This is the story of the man who invented stress. And why the way you were taught about it might be part of the problem.
